def: An AI that doesn't just answer: it plans steps and uses tools (read files, run commands, search the web) in a loop until a task is done, checking its own results along the way.
The cycle an agent repeats: think, pick a tool, run it, read the result, decide what's next. It stops when the task is finished or it needs you.
The software around a model that turns it into an agent: the loop, the tools, the permissions, the memory. root-harness is one; Claude Code is another.
A function the model is allowed to call, described by a name and its parameters. The model asks for it in a structured way; the harness runs it and returns the result.
Model Context Protocol: a standard way to plug tools and data sources into any agent. Write an MCP server once (for GitHub, a database...) and every MCP-aware agent can use it.
A helper agent started by another agent for one focused job (search the code, review a file). It works in its own context and reports back a summary.
How much an agent may do without asking you: ask before each risky action, accept file edits, only plan, or decide on its own (auto).
A packaged set of instructions (and sometimes scripts) that teaches an agent how to do one kind of task well, loaded only when that task comes up.
A shortcut typed with a / (like /model or /compact) that tells the harness to do something, instead of sending text to the model.
A script the harness runs automatically at a given moment (before a tool, after an answer...), for example to block a dangerous command or check the work.
Building software by describing what you want in plain words and letting an AI agent write the code, while you steer, test and review.
A closed space where code runs without being able to touch the rest of your machine or the internet, so a mistake or an attack stays contained.
Large Language Model: a neural network trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next piece of text. Claude, GPT and DeepSeek are LLMs.
The unit a model reads and writes: a word or a piece of word (about 3/4 of an English word on average). Prices and limits are counted in tokens.
The part that cuts text into tokens before the model sees it, and glues tokens back into text after. Each model family has its own.
Everything the model can see at once: instructions, conversation, files, tool results. Measured in tokens; when it's full, older parts must be summarized or dropped.
The text you give a model to get an answer. Clear goal, useful context and an example of the expected result make a big difference.
Hidden instructions given to the model before the conversation, setting its role, rules and tone. You don't see it in the chat, but it shapes every answer.
A setting for randomness. Low: precise and repeatable answers (good for code). High: more varied and creative answers, but more mistakes.
When a model states something false with confidence (a function that doesn't exist, a made-up source). Checking facts and sources is the cure.
When a model works through a problem step by step before answering. It costs more tokens and time, but helps a lot on hard tasks.
How much thinking you allow a model per answer (low to max). More effort: better on hard problems, slower and more expensive.
Using a trained model to produce answers. Training builds the model once; inference is every time you ask it something.
The billions of numbers learned during training that make up the model. '27B' means 27 billion parameters; more usually means smarter but heavier.
A model whose weights you can download and run yourself (Llama, Qwen, Mistral...), unlike models only reachable through a company's API.
Storing a model's weights with fewer bits (8, 4...) so it needs less memory and runs on smaller machines, for a small loss in quality.
A file format for quantized open models, used by llama.cpp and Ollama to run them on an ordinary computer.
Training an existing model a bit more on your own examples so it learns a style or a task. It changes the weights, unlike prompting.
A cheap way to fine-tune: instead of changing all the weights, you train a small add-on layer. Much less memory, and you can swap add-ons.
The neural network design behind almost all LLMs. Its key idea, attention, lets every word look at every other word to understand context.
The mechanism that lets a model weigh which earlier words matter for the current one, like knowing what 'it' refers to in a sentence.
A model that understands more than text: images, audio, sometimes video. You can show it a screenshot and ask about it.
Reusing the already-processed beginning of a prompt (long instructions, documents) across requests, so repeated calls are faster and cheaper.
Summarizing the older part of a long conversation so it fits in the context window again, keeping the important facts and dropping the rest.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation: before answering, the system searches your documents for the relevant passages and gives them to the model, so it answers from your data, not memory.
A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a text. Texts with similar meanings get close embeddings, which is how semantic search works.
A database built to store embeddings and quickly find the ones closest to a question's embedding. The search engine behind most RAG systems.
Cutting documents into smaller pieces before embedding them, so a search returns the precise passage instead of a whole 50-page file.
Searching by meaning rather than exact words: 'how do I get a refund' can find a page titled 'Returns policy'.
A second pass that re-orders search results with a more careful model, so the truly best passages reach the LLM first.
Making a model base its answer on given sources (and cite them) instead of its memory, which greatly reduces hallucinations.
A defined way for programs to talk to each other: you send a request in an agreed format, you get an answer. Models are usually reached through an API.
A secret string that identifies you to a service and bills your usage. Treat it like a password: never in your code, never in a commit.
Software Development Kit: a library that makes using a service easier from your code, instead of writing raw API requests yourself.
A specific address of an API (a URL) that does one thing, like /chat/completions to get an answer from a model.
A simple text format for structured data ({"name": "Root", "age": 8}). Most APIs and tools exchange data in JSON.
The tool that tracks every change to your code, lets you go back in time, and lets many people work on the same project without overwriting each other.
A saved snapshot of your changes in Git, with a message explaining why. Small, clear commits make a project easy to follow.
A parallel line of work in Git. You build a feature on a branch, then merge it back into the main line when it's ready.
A request to merge a branch into another, with a page where people review the changes, discuss and run tests before accepting.
Continuous Integration: tests and checks that run automatically on every push or pull request, so broken code is caught before it's merged.
A project's folder tracked by Git, with its full history. On GitHub, a repository is where the code, issues and pull requests live.
The waiting time between a request and its answer. For AI, time to the first token often matters more than total time.
A regular expression: a compact pattern to find or check text, like ^[a-z]+@ to match the start of an email address.
Capture The Flag: a cybersecurity competition where you solve challenges (break a web app, reverse a program, crack a code) to find hidden secret strings called flags.
The secret string you must find in a CTF challenge (often like FLAG{...}). Submitting it proves you solved the challenge.
A piece of code or a technique that takes advantage of a vulnerability to make a system do something it shouldn't.
A flaw in software that an attacker can use, like a missing check on user input. Fixing it is called patching.
A public ID for a known vulnerability (like CVE-2024-3094), so everyone talks about the same flaw and can check if they're affected.
Taking a compiled program apart to understand how it works without its source code, often with a disassembler like Ghidra.
CTF slang for exploiting a program to take control of it, typically through memory bugs like buffer overflows.
Writing more data into a memory area than it can hold, spilling into neighbouring memory. Classic bug in C that can let an attacker run code.
Slipping database commands into an input field so the app runs them. Prevented by never pasting user input directly into SQL.
Cross-Site Scripting: injecting JavaScript into a web page that other users then run in their browser, for example to steal their session.
Hiding instructions in content an AI reads (a web page, a file, an email) to make it obey the attacker instead of the user. The number one risk for agents.
A prompt crafted to make a model ignore its safety rules. Labs test against them; attackers keep inventing new ones.
Attacking your own system on purpose, like a real adversary would, to find its weaknesses before others do.
Encryption where only the sender and the recipients can read the message: not the servers or relays carrying it, not the app maker.
The half of a key pair you can share freely: people use it to encrypt messages for you or check your signatures. Only your secret key can open them.
A fixed-size fingerprint of data (like SHA-256). The same input always gives the same hash, and you can't get the input back from it.
